title: Critical Thinking and Writing
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Underwood, a former university assessment coordinator, asks where critical thinking comes from and how institutions claim to measure it. He moves from his own schooling and Socrates' suspicion of writing, to a skeptical look at popular treatments that treat critical thinking as an autonomous, solitary skill, to the WICHE Academic Passport and AAC&U VALUE rubric work. He argues that assessing writing and critical thinking at once is unreliable, citing the iPAL framework as an alternative that opens the aperture beyond literacy. Drawing on a survey of about 1,300 faculty, he concludes that learning outcomes do not behave as discrete boxes but overlap like shards in a kaleidoscope. The essay closes by locating critical thinking in dialogic, mentored activity rather than in a white paper or a script.
points: Underwood challenges the idea that critical thinking is an autonomous solitary skill, contrasting a white-paper pitch with mentored early-childhood questioning.
He recalls that Socrates preferred live dialogue to writing because a text cannot answer questions.
Faculty often use writing as evidence of critical thinking, but researchers question the reliability of assessing both at once.
His faculty survey ranked critical thinking highest of fifteen AAC&U outcomes, at about 4.5 of 5 across disciplines.
Outcomes overlap like kaleidoscope shards, so attention belongs on learners in action rather than on fidelity to a script.
quotes: Socrates wanted little to do with writing beyond its use as a memory aid, though he seems to have given in to a bit of Sappho. He preferred two or more live minds creating a critical fire to melt down faulty assumptions in real time.

I’m troubled—not by the White Paper. I haven’t even read it and offer no thoughts on it. What troubles me most is the assumption that critical thinking is somehow autonomous, a solitary force in consciousness.
One danger of writing, as Socrates pointed out, is this: Writing doesn’t answer questions. Ask one and the writing provides no more than what you already have.

Still, when higher education is asked to show evidence that students are actually developing CT, that the institution is not academically adrift, faculty often turn to writing as the source of evidence. Students who are competent writers leave evidentiary traces of critical thinking in their texts, so the thinking goes.

But isn’t it better if the writer keeps the clutter out of the polished text? How does one assess critical thinking in a product built for clarity, coherence, unity, and order, a product intentionally sweeping the mess under the rug?
The most potent outcome driving instruction across the board was Critical Thinking weighing in 4.5ish depending on the discipline with very little variability. Writing was in the top tier.

Learning outcomes double up, bend, overlap, and reposition themselves in the ever changing landscape of a teacher’s consciousness trained on learners in action. It is here attention needs to focus, not on fidelity to a script.
